results.summary: SoilZ v1 is a 1-bit IQ lock-in sigma-delta impedance analyzer for soil moisture sensing, implemented in IHP SG13G2 130nm BiCMOS. It uses a PTAT current source, H-bridge excitation, chopper demodulation, a continuous-time sigma-delta modulator, and a digital divider chain to produce a bitstream whose density is proportional to the impedance between two analog pins. The design is tested by connecting a resistive load or soil probe between ua[0] and ua[1] and counting the bitstream density with an external microcontroller such as an ESP32. Notable features include a 5-stage ring VCO with PTAT bias for temperature compensation and a programmable current source, but no silicon test results are provided.

LoRa Edge SoC is a RISC-V (RV32EC) system-on-chip based on the TinyQV bit-serial CPU, integrating peripherals such as CRC16, I2C master, SPI master, watchdog timer, RTC, and a tamper-detection register. It is intended for LoRa IoT edge nodes, booting from external QSPI Flash and using QSPI PSRAM for data storage, with a UART for debug output. Testing requires connecting QSPI Flash, PSRAM, an SX1268 LoRa module, I2C sensors, and optionally a GPS module, then running firmware to exercise the peripherals. The design is notable for its compact integration of a RISC-V core with LoRa-oriented peripherals, but no silicon test results are reported.

TeenySPU is a 4-bit spatial processing unit that implements a spatial instruction set architecture (SISA) for basic raster data, vector data, and geoAI processing. The design uses 4-bit inputs for operation codes and Q multiplexer codes, with 4-bit outputs for N and M, and bidirectional pins for AC and BD. It can be tested in simulation using the provided Verilog testbench, which covers all operations. The documentation does not specify external hardware requirements or silicon test results, and the design is notable for its compact 4-bit spatial processing approach.

This design is a bit-serial Collatz Conjecture checker that iterates on a number until it reaches 1, counting the number of steps. It consists of a main shift register, a step counter register, and a state machine, with serial input and output for the main register and step register, plus finished and overflow flags. The design does not require external hardware, but the testing procedure is marked as TODO, so no verification details are provided. The bit-serial approach is notable for saving area, but no silicon results or further documentation are available.

Plasma is a VGA animation design that renders a plasma effect with selectable color themes and an optional about text overlay. It uses two input pins to select among four color modes (default, matrix, cyberpunk, abyss) and one input to enable the about overlay, outputting VGA signals on the standard Tiny VGA pinout. The design requires an external TinyVGA PMOD to connect to a VGA monitor. The documentation states that no testing was performed, and no silicon results are provided.

TinyMOA is a RISC-V CPU based on TinyQV with an integrated SRAM-based compute-in-memory accelerator for analog matrix multiplications. The design is currently a work in progress, with no detailed documentation of its operation or testing procedure. It provides debug outputs for the program counter and state, but external hardware requirements are not specified. The project is notable for combining a RISC-V core with an analog compute-in-memory accelerator, but further information is lacking.

Tiny Perceptron implements a hashed perceptron, a hardware-friendly predictor often used for branch prediction, using external SPI RAM to store signed 8-bit weights. It communicates with a host controller via a 16-bit SPI slave interface, supporting operations to add weight indices, read the signed sum, and update weights based on a sign bit. Testing requires an external SPI RAM, such as the SPI RAM emulator on a Raspberry Pi Pico, connected to the bidirectional pins. The design is notable for its use of external RAM and a simple SPI protocol, but no silicon test results are provided.

This design blinks all 16 output pins together to transmit the message "HELLO WORLD" in Morse code at approximately 20 WPM, looping continuously. It requires only LEDs or a logic analyzer connected to any of the output pins and a clock of about 16 Hz. No inputs are used, and the design was written by GitHub Copilot. The project is notable for its simplicity and AI-generated origin, but no silicon test results are reported.

This design implements triple modular redundancy with 8 inputs and 8 outputs, where three external processors communicate via SPI and their outputs are voted on to produce a single output. It includes a shared chip select and clock, with dedicated MISO and MOSI lines for each processor, and uses a majority vote to tolerate faults. Testing involves cocotb simulations that cover valid echo handling, per-bit validity masks, majority voting, and fault injection, and on hardware it requires three external CPUs or SPI slaves. The design is notable for its fault-tolerance approach, but no silicon test results are provided.

This design renders a movable white square on a gray background via VGA, with inputs to move the square left, right, up, and down, and to increase or decrease its size. It uses the standard Tiny VGA pinout and requires an external TinyVGA PMOD and switches for input. The design is intended to mimic moving a cursor on a screen, and no testing or silicon results are documented.
